attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. He presents the passage as a quote from his upcoming premium piece, which is still his writing.

semantics.note: In context, 'It is not capable of building it' refers to typing one broad prompt and getting a fully formed Salesforce competitor. 'From a prompt' keeps that scope. This is a firm present-tense statement about capability.

contract.note: The plain reading (one broad prompt, a usable core CRM, a practical way to run it) is ordinary and fair. Limiting it to the period up to publication fits the context. 'Salesforce competitor' has no stated threshold, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own Nov 2025 engineering post on long-running agents. It describes features marked complete without end-to-end testing and the need for scaffolding. It does not test building a CRM from one prompt.

Anthropic disclosure from Feb 2026 saying Claude Code ordinarily needs an operator online. Relevant to how much autonomy it has, but the demo is a compiler built with a custom harness, not a CRM from one prompt.

reviews.rationale: Both items are company disclosures that only give context on agent limitations. Neither tests a single-prompt CRM build, and the packet has no trial either way. A lack of published successes does not prove incapability, so the evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron is rejecting the Citrini passage he quotes. The denial, 'not something that Claude Code can do', is his own endorsed claim.

semantics.note: The proposition carries over the scope of the quoted passage: a competent developer, core functionality, weeks, and the CIO standard. It also includes his charge that the claim is a lie, which he did make. The scored part is the capability.

contract.note: Allowing developer-assisted, iterative work matches what Citrini claimed and Zitron denied. The buyer-credibility threshold is subjective but taken from the quoted text, and treating the 'lie' charge as not testable is reasonable.

evidence.note: Firsthand Feb 2026 account: most of Linear's core cloned in about 20 prompts over a few evenings. It discloses missing authentication and real-time features, the code is unreleased, and there was no buyer or independent evaluation. This weakens a sweeping denial but does not meet the contradiction standard.

reviews.rationale: The only item is a self-reported demo, close to the claimed capability but with disclosed gaps. It has no independent test or buyer-credibility assessment. No contemporary trials show the standard was out of reach either. The evidence does not settle the claim either way.

attribution.note: The main claim is Zitron's own assertion. The 80% figure paraphrases a study he cites.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the majority claim. The drafter's original_threshold of 'more than 80%' belongs to the cited study's employment and productivity finding, not to the majority claim. The proposition itself is accurate.

contract.note: Reading 'little or no return' as no significant financial benefit is ordinary and fair. Using survey waves from just before publication and checking the cited study separately is reasonable.

evidence.note: PwC survey of 4,454 CEOs, fieldwork ending Nov 2025: 56% report no significant financial benefit from AI to date. This is a majority of CEOs, within the target period. The figures are self-reported.

Confirms a sample of almost 6000 across the four countries, but respondents were CFOs, CEOs and other executives, and the 80% figure is about employment and productivity, not financial return. It does not test the majority-ROI claim.

reviews.rationale: PwC's CEO-only survey shows 56% saw no significant financial benefit from AI, which meets the majority claim on a fair ordinary reading. The cited four-country study was mislabelled as all CEOs and measures employment and productivity, so it serves only as context. The scored majority claim holds.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: The main claim is causal: fear of LLMs took root among investors and pushed incumbent software stocks down. 'Myth' is his characterization and cannot be tested from market data.

contract.note: Requiring that AI fears materially contributed, rather than were the sole cause, over the month before publication is a fair, ordinary reading. Setting aside the 'myth' judgment is reasonable because market evidence cannot settle it.

evidence.note: Reuters, Feb 3 2026: software selloff deepened as traders and analysts cited AI concerns. Salesforce, ServiceNow and Adobe each fell over 5%. It notes SAP's earlier drop followed weak cloud guidance.
Stifel weekly, Feb 6 2026: S&P 500 software index fell 7.8% that week. Stifel links the selloff to fears of AI disrupting incumbent business models.

reviews.rationale: Market data and contemporaneous trader and analyst accounts show substantial incumbent-software declines in the period, attributed largely to AI disruption fears. Part of SAP's fall was guidance-driven, but the SAP example is not part of the scored proposition. Whether the threat is a 'myth' is not scored.
